title: Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013
short_title: Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: Part of a 13-bill package, this bill would ban price exploitation and misleading claims about prices after the carbon tax is repealed.
The bill would create a new offence with fines of up to 6,471 penalty units for companies and 1,295 for individuals, and give the ACCC powers to monitor prices during the transition.
The ACCC would check whether savings from the repeal are passed on to consumers, especially in markets where competition is limited.
changes: Introduce a new prohibition on price exploitation related to the carbon tax repeal for key goods like electricity and gas.
Give the ACCC monitoring powers to assess the effect of the repeal on prices.
Ban false or misleading representations about how the carbon tax repeal affects prices.
summary.affected: Businesses supplying key goods such as electricity and gas, and their customers.

This division relates to the Policies _[For a carbon price](/policies/3)_ and _[For renewable energy](/policies/20)_. The majority voted in favour of a [motion](http://www.openaustralia.org/senate/?gid=2013-12-02.129.1) that: _At the end of the motion that the resumption of debate be made an order of debate for a later hour add: 'and the orders of the day for the resumption of the second reading debate on the Clean Energy Finance Corporation (Abolition) Bill 2013, and subsequently the Climate Change Authority (Abolition) Bill 2013, have precedence over this bill and the other related bills until determined.'_ (You can read the associated debate [here](http://www.openaustralia.org/senate/?id=2013-12-02.127.1). It commenced after 8:38 pm. ) Passing this motion means that the second reading debate about the Clean Energy Finance Corporation (Abolition) Bill 2013 and the Climate Change Authority (Abolition) Bill 2013 will be resumed before the debate about the Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013 and other related bills. The motion was introduced by Labor Senator [Penny Wong](http://publicwhip-rails.openaustraliafoundation.org.au/mp.php?mpn=Penny_Wong&mpc=Senate&house=senate). _Background to the bills_ The Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013 was introduced into Parliament as part of a package of eleven bills to remove the [carbon pricing mechanism](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_pricing_in_Australia) and abolish the [Clean Energy Finance Corporation](http://www.cleanenergyfinancecorp.com.au/about-us.aspx) and the [Climate Change Authority](http://climatechangeauthority.gov.au/about). The eleven bills are: - [Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r5137) - [True-up Shortfall Levy (General) (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r5131)
Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013 and related bills - Second Reading - Protect Australia from climate change

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](http://www.openaustralia.org/senate/?gid=2014-03-17.17.1) introduced by Labor Senator [Jacinta Collins](http://publicwhip-rails.openaustraliafoundation.org.au/mp.php?mpn=Jacinta_Collins&mpc=Senate&house=senate). The motion was for an amendment to be added to the end of the original motion, which was "_That these bills be now read a second time._" The words were: "_but the Senate calls on the Government to recognise the scientific expert consensus regarding [climate change](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change) and that the repeal of the carbon tax must be accompanied by the introduction of serious and comprehensive policies to address climate change._" Since the motion passed, these words will now be added to the original motion. Background to the bills The [Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r5137) and related bills were introduced as a package to remove the [carbon pricing mechanism](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_pricing_in_Australia), which was introduced by the Australian Labor Party while in government. The Coalition described the mechanism as a “carbon tax” and removing it was a key policy platform during the 2013 election.(You can read more about the Coalition's policy to remove the carbon price [here](http://www.liberal.org.au/scrapping-carbon-tax-and-reducing-cost-living). ) The carbon pricing mechanism commenced on 1 July 2012.(For more information on the carbon pricing mechanism and how it works, please see the Clean Energy Regulator’s [website](http://www.cleanenergyregulator.gov.au/Carbon-Pricing-Mechanism/About-the-Mechanism/Pages/default.aspx).) It is an emissions trading scheme that puts a price on carbon emissions. It applies to “liable entities” (a group that includes companies that emit a high level of greenhouse gases). speeches.speaker: Greg Hunt
speeches.brief: Moved the second reading of a bill imposing a true-up shortfall levy to recover overallocated assistance under the Jobs and Competitiveness Program, ensuring businesses are not over- or under-compensated in the 2013 to 2014 financial year.

speeches.speaker: Greg Hunt
speeches.brief: Moved the second reading of a related bill imposing an excise-based true-up shortfall levy to recover the value of overallocated free carbon units issued under the Jobs and Competitiveness Program for the 2013 to 2014 financial year.

speeches.speaker: Christopher Pyne
speeches.brief: Moved a debate management motion to conclude debate on the Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013 and related bills by Thursday this week, arguing the election gave the coalition a mandate with 90 seats to Labor's 55, Labor's worst result since 1903.

speeches.speaker: Bill Shorten
speeches.brief: Argued against the government's carbon tax repeal bills, saying the decade from 2001 to 2010 was the warmest on record, that Direct Action would cost households an estimated $1,200 a year without a legislated cap on emissions, and noted that under Labor wind power generation trebled and 24,000 renewable energy jobs were created.

speeches.speaker: Mark Butler
speeches.brief: Continued opposing the carbon tax repeal bills, saying NASA had confirmed 97 per cent of actively publishing climate scientists agree human activity causes global warming, cited the IPCC's Fifth Assessment Report finding 95 per cent certainty on human-caused climate change, and noted global average surface temperatures had risen by almost 0.9 degrees Celsius since 1880.

speeches.speaker: Alex Hawke
speeches.brief: Supported repealing the carbon tax, saying Sydney households had faced a 57 per cent increase in power bills since 2010, and noted Australia's $25 a tonne carbon price was the highest in the world with no other country imposing an economy-wide carbon tax.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Nikolic
speeches.brief: Supported repealing the carbon tax, citing a 15.3 per cent rise in electricity prices in the first quarter after its introduction and an almost 11 per cent swing to the Liberal Party in his Bass electorate at the 2013 election, and said the tax cost the economy $9 billion.

speeches.speaker: Shayne Neumann
speeches.brief: Opposed repealing the carbon tax, citing a $4.4 million grant that cut the JBS meatworks' carbon price liability by $790,000 a year in his Ipswich electorate, and said the coalition's review had put a $1.2 million LED street lighting grant for Ipswich in jeopardy.

speeches.speaker: Craig Kelly
speeches.brief: Argued that the Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013 would fulfil the coalition's promise to repeal the carbon tax, restore trust and reduce costs, while claiming the tax disadvantaged Australian businesses, consumers and jobs and had negligible effects on global temperatures.

speeches.speaker: Bob Katter
speeches.brief: Argued that emissions trading would burden Australia's coal and aluminium industries, questioned who would benefit from it, and advocated ethanol as a way to reduce transport emissions, citing international use and potential reductions from grain and sugarcane ethanol.

speeches.speaker: Luke Simpkins
speeches.brief: Supported repealing the Clean Energy Act 2011 and associated charges acts, abolishing related assistance and institutions, and using the ACCC to ensure prices fell, arguing the carbon tax harmed households, businesses and jobs and that the election endorsed repeal.

speeches.speaker: Don Randall
speeches.brief: Argued for repealing the carbon tax, citing Alcoa's warning that the tax would cost Australian aluminium producers at least $60 a tonne while its Western Australian refineries had already cut emissions per tonne by more than 20 per cent since 1990 without one, and noted Western Power's own trigger point for changing behaviour was $90 a tonne.

speeches.speaker: John Cobb
speeches.brief: Argued for repealing the carbon tax, citing about 13,000 small businesses in Calare and an example of a $10,000 annual electricity bill rising by $1,000 a year because of the tax.

speeches.speaker: Mark Dreyfus
speeches.brief: Opposed repealing the carbon tax, arguing the science of climate change is settled and defending the scheme's three-year fixed price period, and noted Australia's carbon price has worked since 1 July 2012, comparing it to California's emissions trading scheme covering about 60 per cent of its economy since 1 January 2013 and China's new carbon pricing trials in seven provinces.

speeches.speaker: Scott Buchholz
speeches.brief: Supported repealing the carbon tax, citing government modelling that the carbon price was set to reach $56 a tonne, said scrapping it would leave average households $550 a year better off from 2014 to 2015, and cited an Australian Industry Group survey of 485 businesses that found manufacturing energy costs rose by an average of 14.5 per cent because of the tax.

speeches.speaker: Jill Hall
speeches.brief: Argued that most electricity price rises in New South Wales stemmed from state network costs rather than the carbon price, said Direct Action modelling showed it would cost Australian households $1,200, and quoted Malcolm Turnbull's December 2009 criticism of the then Opposition Leader's shifting positions on emissions trading, alongside 97 per cent scientific agreement on climate change.

speeches.speaker: Kelly O'Dwyer
speeches.brief: Recalled then Prime Minister Gillard's 2010 promise of no carbon tax before it was legislated on 11 October 2012, cited local business examples in the Higgins electorate of sharp bill increases attributed to a 'carbon charge', and said Treasury modelling showed repeal would save households around $550 a year.

speeches.speaker: Natasha Griggs
speeches.brief: Supported the bill to reduce Territory bills and argued that the carbon tax should be repealed, saying it increased costs for households, businesses and local government without delivering environmental benefits. Cited Treasury modelling of an average household cost reduction of around $550 during the 2014-15 financial year and urged Territory representatives to support repeal.

speeches.speaker: Graham Perrett
speeches.brief: Opposed the Clean Energy Legislation (Carbon Tax Repeal) Bill 2013, citing a 6.1 per cent drop in electricity sector emissions equivalent to 12 million tonnes of carbon dioxide, a 30 per cent surge in renewable energy generation, and more than 150,000 jobs created since the carbon price began.

speeches.speaker: Bob Baldwin
speeches.brief: Supported repealing the carbon tax, arguing it had raised $16 billion over two years without reducing domestic emissions, promised families would be $550 a year better off once it is scrapped, and confirmed the government retains the same five per cent emissions reduction target by 2020 that Labor had set.

speeches.speaker: Jim Chalmers
speeches.brief: Opposed repealing the carbon tax, noting that sixty-odd thousand Australians attended climate change rallies around the country on the weekend, including firefighters concerned about the impact on their work, and argued the government's course of cutting the Clean Energy Finance Corporation and scientists' funding is the wrong direction.
